questions.question: For i.i.d. continuous random variables $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ with $n\ge2$, every strict ordering $X_{a_1}<X_{a_2}<\cdots<X_{a_n}$ has probability $\frac{1}{n!}$. Which argument gives this value?
options: Each adjacent comparison $X_{a_k}<X_{a_{k+1}}$ has probability $\tfrac{1}{2}$, and the $n-1$ comparisons multiply.
The common distribution is symmetric about its median, so each ordering is as likely as its reverse.
Swapping labels leaves all probabilities unchanged, so the $n!$ orderings are equally likely, and ties have probability $0$.
Independence alone makes all orderings equally likely, whatever distribution each $X_i$ has.

questions.question: For i.i.d. random variables $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ with $n\ge2$, why does the result $\mathbb{P}(X_{a_1}<\cdots<X_{a_n})=\frac{1}{n!}$ for every ordering require the common distribution to be continuous?
options: Continuity gives $\mathbb{P}(X_i=X_j)=0$ for $i\ne j$, so the $n!$ strict orderings carry all the probability.
Continuity makes the common density symmetric, so large and small values are equally likely.
Continuity makes $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ independent, which a discrete distribution could not guarantee.
Continuity lets each $X_i$ take every value in an interval, so that every ordering can occur.

questions.question: Let $X_1,X_2,X_3$ be i.i.d. $\operatorname{Exp}(\lambda)$ waiting times, a right-skewed distribution. Which statement about $\mathbb{P}(X_1<X_2<X_3)$ is correct?
options: It is below $\tfrac{1}{6}$, because the right skew piles the three values up near $0$.
It equals $\tfrac{1}{6}$ only for a symmetric law, so here it must be found by integration.
It depends on $\lambda$, since a larger rate makes all three waiting times shorter.
It equals $\tfrac{1}{6}$ for every $\lambda>0$, as for any three i.i.d. continuous variables.

questions.question: For i.i.d. continuous random variables $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ with $n\ge2$ and a rank $k\in\{1,\ldots,n\}$, how does $\mathbb{P}(X_1\text{ is the }k\text{th smallest of }X_1,\ldots,X_n)$ depend on $k$?
options: It is largest for $k$ near $\frac{n}{2}$, since typical values sit in the middle.
It equals $\frac{k}{n}$, so it grows with the rank $k$.
It depends on the common distribution, so no single formula holds.

questions.question: Let $X_1,X_2,\ldots$ be i.i.d. continuous random variables. A record is an observation larger than every earlier one, and $X_1$ counts as a record. For $j\ge2$, what is $\mathbb{P}(X_j\text{ is a record})$?
Four i.i.d. continuous measurements $X_1,X_2,X_3,X_4$ are taken. What is the probability that they come out in the order $X_3<X_1<X_4<X_2$?
Three i.i.d. continuous random variables $X_1,X_2,X_3$ are observed. Given that $X_1<X_2$, what is the conditional probability that $X_3>X_2$?

Four i.i.d. continuous observations $X_1,X_2,X_3,X_4$ arrive one by one, and $X_j$ sets a record when it beats all observations before it ($X_1$ always does). How many records are expected among the four?
Five i.i.d. continuous random variables $X_1,\ldots,X_5$ are observed. Ignoring $X_4$ and $X_5$, what is the probability of the event $X_1<X_2<X_3$?
Two fair six-sided dice give independent scores $X_1$ and $X_2$, so $\mathbb{P}(X_1=X_2)=\tfrac{1}{6}$. What is $\mathbb{P}(X_1<X_2)$?

Let $X_1\sim\operatorname{Unif}(0,1)$ and $X_2\sim\operatorname{Unif}(2,3)$ be independent. Which statement correctly names the assumption of the symmetry result that fails and gives $\mathbb{P}(X_1<X_2)$?
options: Identical distribution fails, but $\mathbb{P}(X_1<X_2)=\tfrac{1}{2}$ still holds by independence.

questions.question: Let $X_1\sim\operatorname{Unif}(0,1)$ and $X_2=X_1$, so $X_2$ has the same continuous distribution as $X_1$ but the two are not independent. Which statement about comparing $X_1$ and $X_2$ is correct?
options: $\mathbb{P}(X_1<X_2)=\tfrac{1}{2}$, since both have the same continuous distribution.
$\mathbb{P}(X_1=X_2)=0$, since each of $X_1$ and $X_2$ is continuous.

questions.question: Let $X_1,X_2,\ldots$ be i.i.d. continuous random variables. A record is an observation larger than every earlier one, and $X_1$ counts as a record. How does the expected number of records among $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ behave as $n\to\infty$?
options: It tends to infinity, but slowly, roughly like $\ln n$.
It converges to a finite limit, because the record probabilities $\frac{1}{j}$ tend to $0$.
It grows roughly like $\frac{n}{2}$, since a new observation beats its predecessor half the time.
It converges to $2$, because each new record is half as likely as the previous one.

questions.question: Let $X_1,\ldots,X_5$ be i.i.d. continuous random variables. What is the probability that $X_1$ is the largest and $X_2$ is the smallest of the five?
Let $X_1,X_2,\ldots$ be i.i.d. continuous random variables, and let $N$ be the first index $j\ge2$ at which $X_j$ exceeds all of $X_1,\ldots,X_{j-1}$. What is $\mathbb{P}(N=4)$?
Let $X_1,\ldots,X_{10}$ be i.i.d. continuous random variables. For $2\le j\le9$, call $X_j$ a peak if $X_j>X_{j-1}$ and $X_j>X_{j+1}$. What is the expected number of peaks?

Let $X_1,X_2,\ldots$ be i.i.d. continuous random variables, and let $N$ be the first index $j\ge2$ at which $X_j$ exceeds all of $X_1,\ldots,X_{j-1}$, so $\mathbb{P}(N>n)=\frac{1}{n}$. Which statement about $N$ is correct?
options: $\mathbb{P}(N=\infty)>0$, because $X_1$ may exceed every later observation.
$\mathbb{E}N=3$, since each later observation independently beats $X_1$ with probability $\tfrac{1}{2}$.

questions.question: Let $X_1\sim\operatorname{Unif}(-1,1)$, $X_2\sim\operatorname{Unif}(-2,2)$ and $X_3\sim\operatorname{Unif}(-8,8)$ be independent. Which statement about how these variables are ordered is correct?
options: $\mathbb{P}(X_1<X_2)\ne\tfrac{1}{2}$, because equal chances require identical distributions.
$\mathbb{P}(X_1<X_2)>\tfrac{1}{2}$, because $X_2$ has the wider range and so tends to be larger.
$\mathbb{P}(X_1<X_2)=\tfrac{1}{2}$, even though $X_1$ and $X_2$ are not identically distributed.
All six orderings of $X_1,X_2,X_3$ have probability $\tfrac{1}{6}$, as each pair is ordered either way with probability $\tfrac{1}{2}$.

questions.question: For i.i.d. continuous $X_1,X_2,X_3$, let $I_j$ indicate that $X_j$ exceeds all earlier values ($I_1=1$), and let $R=I_1+I_2+I_3$ count these records. What is $\operatorname{Var}(R)$?
options: It cannot be found from the record probabilities alone, since a record at index $2$ makes one at index $3$ less likely.

questions.question: Let $X_1,\ldots,X_{20}$ be i.i.d. continuous random variables. A record is an observation larger than every earlier one, and $X_1$ counts as a record. What is the probability that none of $X_{11},\ldots,X_{20}$ is a record?
